Title: Rome in World Time, Part 2: The Republic Fights for Italy (509–264 BC)

Summary: In its first 250 years the Roman Republic fought Etruscans, Latins, Samnites, Gauls and a Greek king with war elephants, survived a sack of the city itself, and went through repeated strikes and mutinies by its own poorer citizens. By 264 BC it controlled Italy. In the same span Greece beat Persia, Athens rose and fell, Alexander conquered to India, and China's Warring States fought toward unification.

---

When the kings were gone, Rome was a mid-sized city in central Italy with hostile neighbours on every side. Two and a half centuries later it ruled the whole peninsula south of the Po. This post covers how that happened, the internal fights that nearly tore the Republic apart along the way, and what the rest of the world was doing.

## Fighting for survival (509–390 BC)

The expelled king Tarquin found allies quickly. The Etruscan king **Lars Porsenna** of Clusium marched on Rome in about 508 BC. This is the setting for three famous Roman legends:

- **Horatius Cocles** held the wooden bridge over the Tiber alone while it was cut down behind him.
- **Mucius Scaevola** was caught trying to kill Porsenna and held his right hand in a fire to show Roman toughness.
- **Cloelia**, a hostage, escaped by swimming the Tiber with other girls.

Some ancient writers (Tacitus and Pliny) hint that Porsenna actually captured Rome, which the heroic stories may be covering up.

Next came the **Latins**. Rome beat them at **Lake Regillus** (c. 496 BC, trad.) and signed the **Foedus Cassianum** treaty (493 BC), making Rome the leading partner in a Latin alliance. For most of the 400s BC, Rome fought seasonal wars against hill peoples, the **Aequi** and **Volsci**, and a long rivalry with the Etruscan city of **Veii**, only 15 km away.

- 477 BC: almost the entire Fabian clan (306 men by tradition) was wiped out by Veii at the Cremera river.
- 458 BC: **Cincinnatus** was called from his plough to be dictator, beat the Aequi, and went back to his farm 16 days later.
- 406–396 BC: Rome besieged Veii for ten years (trad.) and took it under **Marcus Furius Camillus**. Rome began paying its soldiers during this siege.

## The sack of Rome by the Gauls (390 BC, or 387/386)

Celtic Gauls had moved into northern Italy. In 390 BC (Roman reckoning; Greek sources point to 387/386) a Gallic army under **Brennus** crushed the Romans at the **Allia** river and sacked the city. Legend says the Capitol held out after the sacred geese woke the defenders during a night attack. When the Romans complained about the Gauls' rigged weights while paying a ransom in gold, Brennus threw his sword onto the scale and said *vae victis*, "woe to the conquered."

The sack was a trauma Romans remembered for 800 years. The next time a foreign enemy took Rome was in AD 410. Afterwards Rome built a much stronger stone wall (the so-called **Servian Wall**, actually built in the 300s BC).

## The Struggle of the Orders: Rome's internal revolution

While fighting outside enemies, Rome was fighting itself. Power was held by the **patricians**, a closed set of old families. Everyone else was a **plebeian**, and many plebeians were in debt bondage. Their main weapon was the strike.

| Year (BC) | Event | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 494 | **First Secession of the Plebs**: the plebeians, who made up the army, walked out of the city to the Sacred Mount and refused to fight | Created the **tribunes of the plebs**, officials who could veto magistrates |
| 485 | Spurius Cassius executed for "aiming at kingship" | The first of many reformers accused of wanting to be king |
| 451–450 | Ten men (decemvirs) write the **Twelve Tables**, Rome's first written law | Law becomes public, not secret patrician knowledge |
| 449 | **Second Secession** after the decemvir Appius Claudius tried to seize Verginia; her father killed her rather than let it happen | The decemvirs fall |
| 445 | Lex Canuleia allows patrician–plebeian marriage | |
| 439 | Spurius Maelius killed for distributing grain, again accused of aiming at kingship | |
| 384 | Marcus Manlius Capitolinus, the hero of the geese, thrown from the Tarpeian Rock for championing debtors | |
| 367 | **Licinian–Sextian laws**: one consul may be plebeian (first in 366) | The ruling class opens up |
| 326 | Debt bondage (*nexum*) abolished (trad. date) | |
| 300 | Lex Ogulnia opens priesthoods to plebeians | |
| 287 | **Third Secession**; Lex Hortensia makes plebeian assembly votes binding on everyone | Ends the Struggle of the Orders |

The result was not democracy. It was a new combined elite, the *nobilitas*, of rich patrician and plebeian families. But the tools forged in these fights, especially the tribunes, were the same ones that reformers like the Gracchi would use 150 years later.

## Conquering Italy (343–264 BC)

| Years (BC) | War | Key moments |
|---|---|---|
| 343–341 | First Samnite War | Rome fights the Samnites of the central Apennines for Campania |
| 342 | **Mutiny of the Capua garrison** | Roman soldiers wintering in rich Capua plotted to seize the city for themselves; the revolt was defused with an amnesty (Livy 7.38–42) |
| 340–338 | **Latin War** | Rome's own allies revolt. Rome wins and dissolves the Latin League |
| 326–304 | Second Samnite War | 321: humiliation at the **Caudine Forks**, where a trapped Roman army was forced to pass under a yoke of spears. Rome later recovers |
| 312 | | Appius Claudius builds the **Via Appia** and Rome's first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia |
| 298–290 | Third Samnite War | 295: **Sentinum**, Rome beats Samnites, Gauls, Etruscans and Umbrians together, the biggest battle in Italy up to then |
| 283 | | Lake Vadimo: Rome defeats Etruscans and Gauls |
| 280–275 | **Pyrrhic War** | King **Pyrrhus** of Epirus, a relative of Alexander, comes to help Tarentum with elephants. He wins at Heraclea (280) and Asculum (279) at such cost that we still say "Pyrrhic victory." Rome beats him at Beneventum (275) |
| 280–270 | **Rogue legion at Rhegium** | A Roman garrison of Campanian troops murdered the townsmen of Rhegium and held the city for ten years. Rome retook it in 270 and executed the survivors in the Forum |
| 272 | | Tarentum surrenders. Rome controls southern Italy |
| 265–264 | | Rome destroys Etruscan Volsinii after its ruling class asked for help against a revolt of former slaves |

How did Rome win? Not by being invincible; it lost plenty of battles. It won because it turned beaten enemies into **allies** who had to supply troops but kept self-government, and planted **colonies** of Roman and Latin settlers at strategic points linked by roads. By 264 BC, Rome could field an enormous pool of manpower, which is exactly what it would need against Carthage.

In 264 BC Rome also held its first recorded **gladiatorial fight**, at a funeral in the Forum Boarium. In the same year it accepted an appeal from the city of Messana in Sicily, which started the First Punic War.

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Rome finished conquering the Latins in the same year Philip of Macedon conquered Greece.** 338 BC was a turning point in both peninsulas, and the two expansions were unconnected.

**Alexander and the Samnite Wars overlapped.** Livy (Book 9, chapters 17–19) wrote a famous "what if" asking whether Alexander would have beaten Rome had he turned west. He concluded, of course, that Rome would have won.

**Salamis and Himera, east and west.** In 480 BC Greeks beat Persia at Salamis and Syracuse beat Carthage at Himera. Six years later Syracuse beat the Etruscans at sea. Rome benefited from all of it without being involved.

**China was fighting its own "conquest of the peninsula."** The Warring States period runs almost exactly parallel to Rome's conquest of Italy. Qin's ruthless reforms under Shang Yang started within a decade of Rome's Licinian-Sextian laws. Both states became machines for turning farmers into soldiers.

**Rome's soldiers mutinied, and plebeians went on strike, long before Spartacus.** The three secessions of the plebs were essentially general strikes by the army. The Capua and Rhegium garrisons show that Roman soldiers sent to rich cities were tempted to keep them.

## What comes next

Part 3 covers the Punic Wars against Carthage, Hannibal crossing the Alps, and Rome's conquest of Greece and Spain, while Qin unites China, the Han dynasty is founded, and Ashoka spreads Buddhism across India.

## Sources and notes

- Livy, *Ab Urbe Condita*, Books 2–10 (to 293 BC). Books 11–20 are lost, so for the Pyrrhic War we rely on summaries and on Plutarch.
- Plutarch, *Life of Pyrrhus* and *Life of Camillus*.
- Polybius, *Histories*, Books 1–2, for the background to the Punic Wars and the Gallic wars.
- Herodotus and Thucydides for the Greek events; Sima Qian, *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian), for Qin and the Warring States.
- T. J. Cornell, *The Beginnings of Rome* (1995), chapters 10–14.
- Overview: [Conflict of the Orders (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_of_the_Orders), [Samnite Wars (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samnite_Wars), [Pyrrhic War (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrrhic_War).

**Flags:** Dates before about 300 BC rely heavily on Livy and are approximate. The Gallic sack is 390 BC in Roman reckoning but more likely 387/386 BC. Many early heroic stories (Horatius, Scaevola, Cincinnatus, the geese) are legends. The start of the Warring States period is conventionally 475 BC, but historians also use 481 or 403 BC. The start of the Yayoi period in Japan is debated, with some scholars placing it centuries earlier.
